message.content:
**Famous Dancers of the 19th Century**

| Name | Nationality | Notable Contributions / Roles |
|------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **Marie Taglioni** (1804–1884) | Swedish/Italian | Pioneered the “en pointe” technique; star of *La Sylphide* (1832). |
| **Fanny Elssler** (1810–1879) | Austrian | Renowned for her virtuosity and dramatic flair; performed across Europe and the U.S. |
| **Marius Petipa** (1818–1910) | Russian | Master choreographer; created many ballets that remain classics (e.g., *Swan Lake*, *The Sleeping Beauty*). |
| **Jean Coralli** (1797–1865) | French | Co‑choreographer of *Giselle* (1841); influential in Parisian ballet. |
| **Carlo Blasis** (1815–1890) | Italian | Developed the “Blasis system,” a foundational method for ballet technique. |
| **Anna Pavlova** (1881–1931) | Russian | Though her career peaked in the early 20th century, she was trained in the 19th‑century tradition and helped popularize ballet worldwide. |
| **John L. T. (John L. T.)** (1810–1885) | American | One of the first American ballet dancers to gain international acclaim. |
| **Eugène Scribe** (1791–1861) | French | While primarily a playwright, his works inspired many 19th‑century dance productions. |
| **Giovanni Battista Viotti** (1755–1824) | Italian | Composer and violinist; his music was often used in ballets of the era. |
| **Friedrich Schiller** (1759–1805) | German | Playwright whose dramas were adapted into ballets; his influence shaped the narrative content of 19th‑century dance. |

These dancers and choreographers were instrumental in shaping ballet and modern dance during the 19th century, establishing techniques, styles, and repertoires that continue to influence performers today.
